blocks.heading: The communication process
blocks.text: The sender originates the message, the message is the information intended, the medium is the channel used, timing concerns when it is sent and received, the receiver is the intended recipient, and feedback is a response indicating receipt or understanding. The elements must work together. A correct message sent through an inaccessible channel fails to reach its receiver. A clear instruction received too late cannot guide the intended action. Feedback can reveal a misunderstanding so the sender can clarify it; merely observing that a system delivered a notification does not prove comprehension. Good communication checks who needs to know, what they need to understand, how to reach them and by when. Use plain wording and relevant detail rather than overload the receiver with unrelated information.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tuli Foods’ supervisor tells the evening shift that tomorrow’s dispatch deadline is noon, uses an accessible staff channel before the shift ends and asks the shift leader to repeat the arrangement. The supervisor is sender, the changed deadline is the message, the staff channel is the medium, the pre-departure contact is timing, the evening shift is receiver and the repeated arrangement is feedback. An incorrect repetition would identify a need for clarification before the error affects delivery.

blocks.heading: Sender
blocks.text: The sender is the person or group originating the message. The sender should identify the intended receiver, purpose and essential information, then choose accessible wording and a suitable medium. Responsibility for clear communication is not fulfilled simply by saying that a notice was sent. The sender can use feedback to identify the need for clarification.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Olina Works’ supervisor informs staff of a revised safety procedure. The supervisor is the sender. Choosing familiar terms and asking staff to explain the change can reveal whether the intended meaning was conveyed.

blocks.heading: Message
blocks.text: The message is the information or meaning the sender intends to convey. It needs sufficient accuracy and detail for the purpose, such as the task, responsible person and deadline. Ambiguous phrases can let different receivers infer different actions. More words do not necessarily improve a message if important instructions are buried in unrelated detail.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tenga Stores replaces “bring the stock soon” with “move these boxes to shelf B before 15:00 today”. The more precise message identifies what, where and when, reducing the scope for conflicting interpretations. The shelf location should still be understandable to the receiver.

blocks.heading: Media
blocks.text: Media are the channels or means used to carry messages; medium is the singular. A phone call, email or noticeboard can carry information in different circumstances. Select a channel using access, urgency, confidentiality, complexity and the need for feedback or a record. The channel is distinct from the message’s actual content.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Kara Repairs uses a phone call to tell an absent technician about an urgent schedule change. The call is the medium, while the revised schedule is the message. An email account the technician cannot access would be a poor alternative for the stated urgency.

blocks.heading: Timing
blocks.text: Timing concerns when communication is sent, received and available for action. A clear and accurate instruction can fail if it reaches the receiver after the decision or task. Too many messages at a busy moment can also reduce attention. Allow time for access, clarification and the required response rather than treating the sending time as the entire process.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hano Foods’ workers need a revised start time before leaving the previous shift. Giving the update after they arrive the next day is too late to change that arrival. Send and confirm it while they can still adjust their plans.

blocks.heading: Receiver
blocks.text: The receiver is the intended person or group to whom the message is directed. Effective communication depends on reaching the right receiver and on their ability to understand and act. The receiver may need clarification and should provide feedback where appropriate. Sending the information to someone with no relevant responsibility may not achieve the intended action.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tuli Metals needs its purchasing officer to change an order but sends the request only to a salesperson. The purchasing officer is the intended action receiver. Unless the salesperson reliably passes it on, the required decision may not happen.

blocks.heading: Feedback
blocks.text: Feedback is the receiver’s response to a message, which helps the sender assess receipt, understanding or reaction. A question can reveal ambiguity; repeating an instruction in the receiver’s own words can reveal a mistaken detail. An electronic delivery notification confirms transmission to a system, not necessarily human understanding. Feedback can be verbal, written or observable action appropriate to the message.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nela Foods’ worker repeats the new deadline as Friday although the supervisor intended Thursday. The incorrect repetition is useful feedback: it reveals a misunderstanding while the sender can still clarify. Silence would not provide the same evidence of understanding.
